aov-installation.meta_desc: AOV Installation for landlords, agents and building managers: vents that open on a signal to clear smoke from stairs and corridors. Request a quote — POA.
aov-installation.intro: AOV Installation: vents that open on a signal to clear smoke from stairs and corridors. iComply works on buildings across the UK mainland from its Stockport workshop, measures before it specifies, and quotes every job price on application. Installation is quoted after measurement and product selection from published data.
aov-installation.body:
An automatic opening vent, usually shortened to AOV, is a window, roof hatch or louvre that opens on a signal so smoke can leave a common stair, corridor or lobby. In most blocks the signal comes from a smoke detector on the same level or from the fire alarm panel. The vent itself is only one part of the job. The actuator, the control panel, the battery standby, the cabling and the firefighter override switch all have to work together before the vent does what the fire strategy expects.

Most AOVs in residential blocks sit at the head of the stair or on each corridor. Guidance in Approved Document B for common stairs and corridors in flats refers to minimum free areas, commonly quoted as 1.0 m² at the stair head and 1.5 m² for a corridor or lobby vent. The fire strategy for the building decides what applies. iComply records the vent size and opening as measured on site and does not assume a free area that has not been checked against the drawings or the maker's data.

An AOV that will not open is a fire-safety defect, not a cosmetic one. The responsible person under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 has to keep fire-safety equipment in efficient working order. That covers smoke vents. In practice it means a written test regime, a log of faults and someone competent to put them right. iComply writes the scope for that work and quotes it on application.

Installation of a AOV starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the AOV works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A AOV that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

AOV repair starts with finding the cause. A symptom — something that will not open, will not close, shows a fault or makes a noise — can have several causes. The fault is reproduced on site and traced before any part is ordered, so the repair fixes the problem rather than a guess.

Repairs use parts that match the original performance from the maker's published data, or a documented equivalent where the original is no longer available. The part used and the reason for the choice are written in the job record.

Some faults leave equipment unsafe or out of service. Where that happens, the equipment is made safe and the responsible person is told in writing what is out of service and what interim measures are needed until the repair is complete.

Where a panel serves more than one zone, the zoning is checked against the fire strategy. A panel that opens every vent in the building on one detector may not match the design intent. Equally, a zone that never opens the stair-head vent is a problem. The cause-and-effect table is written out and agreed before reprogramming.

Replacing a window that is also an AOV needs care. The new frame, sash and hinges must suit the actuator and give at least the free area required. Window installers and smoke-vent engineers need to talk before the order goes in. iComply writes the joint scope so the vent is not lost in a window replacement.

AOV and smoke control work is usually instructed by a landlord, freeholder, managing agent or facilities manager. A commercial tenant may instruct it where the lease requires. The reply confirms whether another party needs to approve the scope.

Typical buildings include purpose-built blocks of flats, converted houses split into flats, care homes, student accommodation, offices, hotels, mixed-use schemes, warehouses and enclosed car parks. Each has its own fire strategy and its own constraints on access.

Smoke control interacts with the fire alarm, door closers, lifts and sometimes the building management system. The visit records those interfaces so faults that cross between systems are traced to the right place.

Buildings change over their life: new partitions, refurbished common parts, changed uses. Where a change could affect smoke control, it is noted for the responsible person and, if needed, the fire engineer.

Occupied buildings mean residents, staff or visitors. Testing that opens vents or sounds alarms is arranged with notice, and work is planned so escape routes stay usable.

Quotes are price on application. iComply does not publish catalogue prices for smoke-control work because two buildings with the same vent can need very different access, testing and interface work. The written scope sets out what is included so the price can be judged fairly.

To start, send the address, the type of building, what is installed (photos of the panel and vents help), any previous service records and the reason for the enquiry. Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form.

iComply does not claim accreditation badges it does not hold, and does not describe products by ratings their makers have not published. Figures in a scope come from site measurement or the maker's documents.

Handover documents typically include the scope, the test results, a list of defects with priorities, photos where useful and any maker's documentation supplied. They are written to be filed in the building's fire-safety records.

What is included in AOV installation?
Survey, product selection from published data, fixing and setting-up, testing, and a handover record. The written scope lists exactly what is included and what is not.
Can installation be phased?
Yes, where a site has to stay in use. The scope sets out each phase and what remains in service.
What does an AOV actually do?

It opens on a signal so smoke can leave a stair, corridor or lobby and the escape route stays usable for longer. The signal usually comes from a local smoke detector or the fire alarm panel, and a firefighter switch lets the fire service override it.

The fire strategy or the O&M manual sets the routine. Many buildings run a short user test weekly or monthly and a full service by a competent engineer at least once a year. iComply follows the building's own regime and writes the results down.

smoke-control-installation.body:
Smoke control is the set of measures that keeps escape routes and firefighting access usable for longer in a fire. In most property work that means smoke vents, smoke shafts, smoke curtains, pressurisation or mechanical extract, depending on the design. Each building's fire strategy sets the approach, and the installed system is judged against it.

BS 7346-8 is the usual code of practice for planning, design, installation, commissioning and maintenance of smoke control systems. The BS EN 12101 series covers the products, such as natural ventilators, powered ventilators, smoke barriers and power supplies. BS 9991 and BS 9999 cover fire safety in the design of residential and non-residential buildings. These are reference points; the building's own strategy is what the work follows.

Smoke control work in an occupied building is about sequence as much as equipment. Detection, vents, fans, dampers, doors and lifts may all have a role. iComply maps the cause-and-effect for the system on site, tests each step, and records what happened against what the strategy expects.

Many smoke control systems were installed by one contractor and maintained by another. Records go missing in between. The first visit often rebuilds the basics: what is installed, where the panel is, what the zones are and when the last service was. That baseline makes every later visit quicker and more useful.

Responsible persons need evidence, not reassurance. The output from a smoke control visit is a written record of what was tested, what passed, what failed and what was done about it. Defects are listed with a recommended action and a priority, and remedial work is quoted on application.

Installation of a smoke control starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the smoke control works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A smoke control that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

Commissioning a smoke control proves that it works as designed, in the building it is installed in, with the interfaces it depends on. It is more than switching on: every function is tested, every interface is proved and the results are recorded.

Commissioning works from a written cause-and-effect or functional description. Where none exists, one is drawn up from the design and agreed before testing starts, so everyone knows what a pass looks like.

Results are recorded item by item. Failures are fixed and retested, and the record shows both. The final commissioning record goes into the building's file with the maker's documentation.

Recommissioning is needed after significant changes: a new panel, a change of interface, an extension. The scope says what will be retested and why.

Smoke ventilation interacts with doors. A self-closing door that is wedged open can wreck the airflow the design relies on. Door issues spotted during the visit are recorded for the responsible person even when they sit outside the smoke-vent scope.

Commissioning an AOV system means proving every cause and effect, not just pressing the test button once. NSHEVS installation covers roof or high-level ventilators, low-level inlets, actuators, controls and power, all chosen from published data to match the design.

NSHEVS stands for natural smoke and heat exhaust ventilation system. It uses buoyancy to let hot smoke leave through high-level vents while replacement air enters lower down. NSHEVS is common in warehouses, factories, atria and shopping centres, as well as in residential stairs. The ventilators themselves are covered by BS EN 12101-2.

An NSHEVS needs inlet air as much as it needs outlets. If the low-level inlets do not open, the roof vents cannot clear smoke properly. Doors, louvres or windows used as inlets are therefore part of the system and part of the test.

Large roof ventilators on industrial buildings are often opened by pneumatic or electric actuators. Pneumatic systems need their gas bottles, valves and pipework checked; electric systems need the panel, cabling and battery checked. The survey notes which type is installed before the service is scoped.

Roof access on industrial NSHEVS is a planning item in its own right. Fragile roof sheets, rooflights and edge protection all affect how ventilators are reached. iComply writes the access method into the scope and does not send anyone onto a roof without it.

The design of an NSHEVS is based on fire size, ceiling height and smoke reservoir layout. Changes to racking, mezzanines or partitions can affect how the system performs. Changes seen on site are reported so the fire engineer can review them if needed.

Commissioning and annual service records for NSHEVS are often thin. The service visit writes down each ventilator, its actuator type, its test result and any defect, so the responsible person has a usable record for insurers and the fire authority.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the NSHEVS works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

AOVs for flats are usually on the common stair and corridors. The building's fire strategy and Approved Document B guidance for blocks of flats set what is expected; the survey records what is installed.

An AOV that will not open is a fire-safety defect, not a cosmetic one. In practice it means a written test regime, a log of faults and someone competent to put them right. iComply writes the scope for that work and quotes it on application.

The sequence on a typical natural smoke shaft or stair system is simple to describe and easy to get wrong. A detector sees smoke. The panel opens the vent on the fire floor and the vent at the top of the stair or shaft. Lift and door interfaces may follow. A firefighter switch at ground level lets the fire service open or close vents by hand. Each step is tested on its own and then end to end, and the result is written down.

Common faults on older AOVs include a dead standby battery, a seized chain actuator, a vent that opens but will not close, a detector head painted over during redecoration and a panel showing a fault that nobody has reset. This page sets out what a AOV is, where it is used and what decides whether it suits a particular building or entrance. It is written for landlords, managing agents, facilities managers and site owners who need to make a decision and want the facts first.

The first step with any AOV is to describe the site: the address, the building or entrance, who uses it and what is installed now. Photos and rough measurements help. iComply then confirms what a visit would look at and what would be left out.

Options are set out side by side in a written scope. Where there is a choice between products, the published manufacturer data for each is named so the comparison is fair. Prices are on application once the scope is agreed.

After a repair, the AOV is tested in normal operation, and any related safety function is retested. The record shows the fault found, the cause, the repair and the test result.

Recurring faults are treated differently from one-offs. If the same fault keeps coming back, the record history is reviewed and the root cause is looked for — a supply problem, a damaged part elsewhere, an installation issue — rather than resetting it again.

The AOV control panel is the brain of a smoke-vent system. It reads the detectors, drives the actuators, charges the standby battery and reports faults. When the panel fails, every vent it controls is suspect, which is why panel faults are treated as priority defects in most fire-safety files.

A window AOV is an opening window fitted with an actuator so it can open automatically for smoke ventilation. It is the most common AOV in blocks of flats, usually on the stair or at the end of a corridor. The window must open far enough, in the right direction, to give the free area the fire strategy relies on.

aov-emergency-repair.meta_desc: AOV Emergency Repair for landlords, agents and building managers: vents that open on a signal to clear smoke from stairs and corridors. Request a quote — POA.
aov-emergency-repair.intro: This AOV Emergency Repair guide explains vents that open on a signal to clear smoke from stairs and corridors, what decides the right approach for buildings across the UK mainland, and how iComply scopes the work before anything is ordered. Emergency calls are treated as priority instructions; no attendance time is promised.
aov-emergency-repair.body:
An automatic opening vent, usually shortened to AOV, is a window, roof hatch or louvre that opens on a signal so smoke can leave a common stair, corridor or lobby. In most blocks the signal comes from a smoke detector on the same level or from the fire alarm panel. The vent itself is only one part of the job. The actuator, the control panel, the battery standby, the cabling and the firefighter override switch all have to work together before the vent does what the fire strategy expects.

Most AOVs in residential blocks sit at the head of the stair or on each corridor. Guidance in Approved Document B for common stairs and corridors in flats refers to minimum free areas, commonly quoted as 1.0 m² at the stair head and 1.5 m² for a corridor or lobby vent. The fire strategy for the building decides what applies. iComply records the vent size and opening as measured on site and does not assume a free area that has not been checked against the drawings or the maker's data.

AOV work is often split between people who never meet. A window installer fits the frame, an electrician runs the cables, a fire-alarm contractor programmes the panel and a managing agent books the tests. iComply prefers one written scope that names every interface, so a vent that fails on test has an owner and a fix rather than a chain of emails.

Emergency AOV repair means a fault that leaves equipment unsafe, out of service, or stuck in a way that affects safety or access. The call is treated as a priority instruction, but no attendance time is promised on this page. The visit is arranged by phone and confirmed in writing.

The first aim on an emergency visit is to make safe: isolate, secure or set the equipment to a safe state, and tell the responsible person in writing what is out of service and what interim measures are needed.

Once safe, the fault is traced and repaired if parts allow. If parts need ordering, the record says so and the follow-up repair is quoted on application.

Emergency faults often reveal underlying issues. After the immediate repair, the record recommends any further checks so the same fault is less likely to recur.

Commissioning a AOV proves that it works as designed, in the building it is installed in, with the interfaces it depends on. It is more than switching on: every function is tested, every interface is proved and the results are recorded.

Commissioning works from a written cause-and-effect or functional description. Where none exists, one is drawn up from the design and agreed before testing starts, so everyone knows what a pass looks like.

Results are recorded item by item. Failures are fixed and retested, and the record shows both. The final commissioning record goes into the building's file with the maker's documentation.

Recommissioning is needed after significant changes: a new panel, a change of interface, an extension. The scope says what will be retested and why.

Seals, hinges and handles age. A window that has dropped on its hinges catches on the frame and the actuator stalls. A handle that has been locked shut by a resident or cleaner stops the vent opening at all. These simple faults are checked first.

The AOV control panel is the brain of a smoke-vent system. It reads the detectors, drives the actuators, charges the standby battery and reports faults. When the panel fails, every vent it controls is suspect, which is why panel faults are treated as priority defects in most fire-safety files.

AOV and smoke control work is usually instructed by a landlord, freeholder, managing agent or facilities manager. A commercial tenant may instruct it where the lease requires. The reply confirms whether another party needs to approve the scope.

Typical buildings include purpose-built blocks of flats, converted houses split into flats, care homes, student accommodation, offices, hotels, mixed-use schemes, warehouses and enclosed car parks. Each has its own fire strategy and its own constraints on access.

Smoke control interacts with the fire alarm, door closers, lifts and sometimes the building management system. The visit records those interfaces so faults that cross between systems are traced to the right place.

Records are often the weakest part of a smoke-control installation. iComply's visit leaves a plain record of what is installed, what was tested and what needs attention, so the next visit starts from facts.

Occupied buildings mean residents, staff or visitors. Testing that opens vents or sounds alarms is arranged with notice, and work is planned so escape routes stay usable.

To start, send the address, the type of building, what is installed (photos of the panel and vents help), any previous service records and the reason for the enquiry. Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form.

iComply does not claim accreditation badges it does not hold, and does not describe products by ratings their makers have not published. Figures in a scope come from site measurement or the maker's documents.

The workshop is at 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE. Sites across the UK mainland are quoted from there, with travel included in the written quote.

Handover documents typically include the scope, the test results, a list of defects with priorities, photos where useful and any maker's documentation supplied. They are written to be filed in the building's fire-safety records.

Where a building's fire strategy is unclear or missing, iComply records what is installed and how it behaves and recommends the responsible person consult a fire engineer on design questions. Design decisions are not made on the fly during a service visit.

faq: What happens first on an emergency visit?
The equipment is made safe and the responsible person is told in writing what is out of service.
What does an AOV actually do?

It opens on a signal so smoke can leave a stair, corridor or lobby and the escape route stays usable for longer. The signal usually comes from a local smoke detector or the fire alarm panel, and a firefighter switch lets the fire service override it.
How often should an AOV be tested?

The fire strategy or the O&M manual sets the routine. Many buildings run a short user test weekly or monthly and a full service by a competent engineer at least once a year. iComply follows the building's own regime and writes the results down.
Can you tell me the free area of my vents?
Only from measurement and the maker's published data. iComply records the opening on site and compares it with the drawings or fire strategy. A free area is never guessed from the look of the window.
Do you guarantee an emergency attendance time?
No attendance time is promised here. Emergency calls are treated as priority instructions and arranged by phone, confirmed in writing.
How do I ask for AOV Emergency Repair?

Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form. Send the address, photos and what you need. The reply is price on application. Workshop: 17 Woodlands Park Road, Offerton, Stockport, Cheshire SK2 5DE.

smoke-curtain-installation.body:
Smoke curtain installation needs the opening size, the head box space above the ceiling and the fixing substrate confirmed on site before a curtain is ordered.

A smoke curtain is a fabric barrier that drops on a signal to stop smoke spreading through an opening, such as a lift lobby, an atrium edge or a shop front. When not needed, it sits rolled in a head box above the ceiling. BS EN 12101-1 is the product standard for smoke barriers, and the maker's data says what each curtain is tested for.

Smoke curtains rely on gravity, a motor and a control unit. Most are designed to deploy on power failure so a dead supply does not leave the opening unprotected. The control unit, the battery and the drop are tested together, and the curtain is raised again to prove it resets.

The most common faults are a curtain that snags on the way down, a bottom bar that does not reach the floor, side guides knocked out of line and a head box obstructed by new ceiling work. Clearance below the curtain is checked so nothing stored or fitted stops it reaching its deployed position.

Fabric condition matters. Tears, stains and heat damage reduce performance. The curtain is run down fully during the visit so the whole length can be inspected, not just the part visible at the head box.

Smoke curtains are often linked to the fire alarm. That interface is part of the test. The curtain should deploy on the right zone and stay deployed until reset. Where the link has been lost during alarm upgrades, it is recorded as a defect.

Installation of a smoke curtain starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the smoke curtain works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

barrier-installation.name: Barrier Installation
barrier-installation.meta_desc: Barrier Installation for car parks, estates and private sites: manual, automatic, height and width barriers sized from measurements. Request a quote — POA.
barrier-installation.intro: Barrier Installation from iComply Property Services covers manual, automatic, height and width barriers sized from measurements. This guide is written for entrances across the UK mainland, starting from a site survey and a written scope rather than a catalogue price. Installation is quoted after measurement and product selection from published data.
barrier-installation.body:
Vehicle barriers control access to car parks, estates, yards and private roads. The main families are manual barriers opened by a keyholder, automatic rising-arm barriers opened by fob, card, keypad, intercom or ANPR, height restriction barriers that keep tall vehicles out, and width restrictors that keep wide vehicles out. Many entrances use two of these together.

Every barrier job starts with measurement. The clear opening between kerbs, walls or islands sets the arm length. The headroom above the barrier position decides whether a straight rising arm can open fully or whether an articulated, folding or swing arm is needed. The ground, buried services, turning space and pedestrian routes decide where the post and foundations can go.

Arm lengths and operator ratings come from the manufacturer's published ranges. Typical UK rising arms run roughly from 3 m to 8 m depending on the model, but that is a range across the market, not a promise for any one product. iComply names the model and quotes its published figures in the scope, and does not invent ratings.

Manual barriers and automatic barriers fail in different ways. Manual barriers lose their counterbalance, seize at the pivot or lose their locks and keys. Automatic barriers add springs, motors, control boards, loops, photocells and access-control interfaces. Diagnosis on site separates the mechanical, electrical and access-control causes before any part is ordered.

Height and width restrictions are often the real reason a barrier is needed. A car park under a building may need a height bar to protect the structure; an estate road may need a width restrictor to keep vans and lorries out. The restriction figure is measured on site, justified by the vehicles the site wants to admit, and shown on signage before the entrance.

Installation of a vehicle barrier starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the vehicle barrier works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A vehicle barrier that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

A vehicle barrier records what is on site in measured terms: dimensions, clearances, ground, existing equipment and constraints. It is the basis for any specification or quote.

The survey output is a written report with measurements, photos and notes. It names what can be installed and what limits the options.

Surveys are useful on their own — for budgeting, for tendering, or for confirming whether an existing installation meets the site's needs.

Survey work is quoted on application. The report belongs to the client and can be used with any installer.

Arm profile matters as well as length. Round, octagonal and rectangular arm sections behave differently in weight and stiffness, and each manufacturer lists which profiles its operators accept at which lengths. A replacement arm that is the right length but the wrong profile may not fit the clamp or may upset the balance.

Signs fixed above the entrance — height limits, car park names, CCTV warnings — are obstructions too. They are measured with everything else, and where a sign sits in the arm's path the sign is usually moved rather than the barrier compromised.

Opening width and clear width are different measurements. The opening width is the full gap between the structures either side of the entrance. The clear width is what vehicles actually have to drive through once the barrier post, rest post, kerbs and any islands are in place. Barrier choice depends on the clear width.

Height barriers are frequently paired with a rising-arm barrier: the height bar stops a tall vehicle before it reaches the entrance, and the rising arm controls who enters. Spacing between the two allows a car to wait without blocking the road and gives tall vehicles room to turn.

Barrier work is usually instructed by a site owner, managing agent, facilities manager or estate manager. On shared sites, the reply confirms who else needs to agree the scope — for example a freeholder or a residents' company.

Typical sites include private car parks, residential estates, office and retail car parks, warehouse yards, depots, schools, hospitals, farms and private access roads. Each has its own traffic, users and constraints.

Barriers sit where vehicles and pedestrians meet. The layout keeps people out of the arm's path where possible, with a separate footway and clear markings.

Ground conditions decide foundations. Buried services are checked before any digging, and the barrier position may move to avoid them.

Signage and markings tell drivers what to expect: access method, height or width limit, contact details. They are part of the scope, not an afterthought.

Records list the barrier model, arm length, settings, measured clearances and test results, so future repairs and replacements start from facts.

Quotes are price on application. Barrier jobs vary with ground, cabling, access control and safety measures, so a catalogue price would mislead. The written scope lists measurements, products and exclusions so the price can be judged fairly.

To start, send the address, photos of the entrance from both directions, rough measurements of the opening and any headroom limits, how many vehicles use it and what you want the barrier to achieve. Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form.

Dimensions in a scope are either measured on site or taken from the manufacturer's published data for the named product. iComply never invents a product rating, and does not describe a barrier as impact-tested unless its maker publishes that classification.

Handover documents include the measured layout, the product and arm details, spring or counterbalance settings, safety test results for powered barriers, and signage details.

The deeper barrier guides on this site cover manual barriers, arm length, height clearance and height restriction, and opening, lane and width restriction. Each links back to a written-scope approach and price on application.

Boom barrier and parking barrier are common names for the same family of rising-arm barriers. The boom is the arm; it lifts to let vehicles pass and lowers behind them.

Boom length is set from the measured clear opening and chosen from the manufacturer's published arm range for the operator. Long booms need a rest post and suitable springs.

Boom barriers can be manual or automatic. Manual booms suit occasional access; automatic booms suit regular traffic with fob, card, ticket or ANPR access.

Boom barriers are sold in a wide range of duties and lengths. Matching the boom length to the measured clear opening and the operator's published range avoids the commonest problems — a boom that bounces, an operator that strains, or a boom that does not reach the rest post.

Many car parks also need a height restriction, either because of a low structure or to keep vans and caravans out. The height is measured and signed; the barrier and height bar are positioned together.

Undercroft and multi-storey car parks often have limited headroom at the entrance. Articulated or swing arms may be needed. Clearances are measured before specifying.

Car park barriers work hard. Springs, arms, loops and access control are checked regularly. Faults are diagnosed on site before parts are ordered.

Signage at car park barriers explains access, height limits and contact details. It is reviewed as part of installation and service.

Choosing a car park barrier installer is mostly about how they handle the parts before and after the fitting. A good installer measures before ordering, names the product and its published data, explains interfaces with other systems, and leaves a written record at the end.

NSHEVS stands for natural smoke and heat exhaust ventilation system. It uses buoyancy to let hot smoke leave through high-level vents while replacement air enters lower down. came-barrier-installation.body:
CAME is an Italian manufacturer of automatic barriers, gates and access control, and its barriers are common on UK car parks, estates and commercial sites. iComply works on CAME barriers to the maker's published instructions and data. This page does not claim CAME accreditation or dealer status.

CAME publishes the arm lengths, duty and accessories supported by each barrier model. The clear opening is measured on site and the model is chosen from those published figures.

Installation covers foundations, the barrier cabinet, arm, rest post, loops or photocells, access control and commissioning to CAME's instructions. Spring settings are matched to the arm length and accessories.

Existing CAME barriers may need new arms, springs, control boards or accessories. Parts are matched from CAME's published data for the model fitted.

Safety devices are set from a risk assessment, with BS EN 12453 as the usual reference for powered barriers.

Commissioning records the model, arm length, spring setting and safety test results.

Installation of a CAME barrier starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the CAME barrier works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A CAME barrier that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

Arm skirts hang below the arm to discourage pedestrians and cyclists from ducking underneath. They add weight and catch air, and they need clearance from the ground when the arm is down. Where a skirt is wanted, it is included in the balance calculation and the arm length is checked against the manufacturer's published limits with the skirt fitted.

A rising arm needs vertical clearance roughly equal to its arm length when fully open, plus the height of the barrier housing. A 4 m arm needs around 4 m of clear headroom above the pivot. In an undercroft, a basement car park or under a canopy, that headroom often does not exist.

Entry and exit lanes behave differently. An entry lane needs room for a car to stop at a reader or intercom without its tail blocking the road; an exit lane needs space for a loop before the arm so the barrier opens as the car arrives. Lane widths, loop positions and stopping distances are marked on the layout drawing.

Signage and markings tell drivers what to expect: access method, height or width limit, contact details. They are part of the scope, not an afterthought.

Records list the barrier model, arm length, settings, measured clearances and test results, so future repairs and replacements start from facts.

The actuator, the control panel, the battery standby, the cabling and the firefighter override switch all have to work together before the vent does what the fire strategy expects.

The sequence on a typical natural smoke shaft or stair system is simple to describe and easy to get wrong. A detector sees smoke. The panel opens the vent on the fire floor and the vent at the top of the stair or shaft. Lift and door interfaces may follow. A firefighter switch at ground level lets the fire service open or close vents by hand. Each step is tested on its own and then end to end, and the result is written down.

AOV work is often split between people who never meet. A window installer fits the frame, an electrician runs the cables, a fire-alarm contractor programmes the panel and a managing agent books the tests. iComply prefers one written scope that names every interface, so a vent that fails on test has an owner and a fix rather than a chain of emails.

care-home-nshevs-installation.body:
NSHEVS stands for natural smoke and heat exhaust ventilation system. It uses buoyancy to let hot smoke leave through high-level vents while replacement air enters lower down. NSHEVS is common in warehouses, factories, atria and shopping centres, as well as in residential stairs. The ventilators themselves are covered by BS EN 12101-2.

An NSHEVS needs inlet air as much as it needs outlets. If the low-level inlets do not open, the roof vents cannot clear smoke properly. Doors, louvres or windows used as inlets are therefore part of the system and part of the test.

Large roof ventilators on industrial buildings are often opened by pneumatic or electric actuators. Pneumatic systems need their gas bottles, valves and pipework checked; electric systems need the panel, cabling and battery checked. The survey notes which type is installed before the service is scoped.

Roof access on industrial NSHEVS is a planning item in its own right. Fragile roof sheets, rooflights and edge protection all affect how ventilators are reached. iComply writes the access method into the scope and does not send anyone onto a roof without it.

The design of an NSHEVS is based on fire size, ceiling height and smoke reservoir layout. Changes to racking, mezzanines or partitions can affect how the system performs. Changes seen on site are reported so the fire engineer can review them if needed.

Commissioning and annual service records for NSHEVS are often thin. The service visit writes down each ventilator, its actuator type, its test result and any defect, so the responsible person has a usable record for insurers and the fire authority.

Installation of a NSHEVS starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the NSHEVS works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A NSHEVS that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

Commissioning a NSHEVS proves that it works as designed, in the building it is installed in, with the interfaces it depends on. It is more than switching on: every function is tested, every interface is proved and the results are recorded.

Commissioning works from a written cause-and-effect or functional description. Where none exists, one is drawn up from the design and agreed before testing starts, so everyone knows what a pass looks like.

Results are recorded item by item. Failures are fixed and retested, and the record shows both. The final commissioning record goes into the building's file with the maker's documentation.

Recommissioning is needed after significant changes: a new panel, a change of interface, an extension. The scope says what will be retested and why.

The free area of each vent is a design figure. iComply records the opening as measured and compares it with the design or the maker's data where available. Where they differ, the difference is reported.

The most common faults are a curtain that snags on the way down, a bottom bar that does not reach the floor, side guides knocked out of line and a head box obstructed by new ceiling work. Clearance below the curtain is checked so nothing stored or fitted stops it reaching its deployed position.

Care homes often use progressive horizontal evacuation, moving residents away from a fire into protected areas rather than straight outside. Smoke control, including a NSHEVS, helps keep those protected routes usable for longer.

Testing in care homes is planned with the manager. Alarms and vents opening can distress residents, so times, notice and areas are agreed in advance.

Care home inspections look for evidence of maintenance. Records that clearly show what was tested and when support the home's fire risk assessment.

Corridors in care homes fill with equipment — hoists, trolleys, chairs. Anything blocking a vent or detector is recorded and reported.

Quotes are price on application. iComply does not publish catalogue prices for smoke-control work because two buildings with the same vent can need very different access, testing and interface work. The written scope sets out what is included so the price can be judged fairly.

To start, send the address, the type of building, what is installed (photos of the panel and vents help), any previous service records and the reason for the enquiry. Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form.

iComply does not claim accreditation badges it does not hold, and does not describe products by ratings their makers have not published. Figures in a scope come from site measurement or the maker's documents.

Where a building's fire strategy is unclear or missing, iComply records what is installed and how it behaves and recommends the responsible person consult a fire engineer on design questions. Design decisions are not made on the fly during a service visit.

commercial-aov-actuator-installation.intro: This Commercial AOV Actuator Installation guide explains the motor that opens and closes the vent to its published force and stroke, what decides the right approach for commercial buildings, and how iComply scopes the work before anything is ordered. commercial-aov-actuator-installation.body:
The actuator is the motor that physically opens and closes the vent. Chain actuators push window sashes outwards. Linear or spindle actuators lift roof hatches and louvre blades. Each one is sized by its maker for a force, a stroke and a supply voltage, and those published figures decide which actuator suits which vent.

Most actuator faults show up as a vent that opens slowly, opens part-way, stalls or will not close. Causes include a worn chain, a bent bracket, a sash that has dropped on its hinges, paint on the slide, or low voltage at the end of a long cable run. The fix depends on the cause, so the vent is opened and closed under test before any part is ordered.

Replacing an actuator means matching the original performance, not just the mounting holes. The stroke has to deliver the required opening, the force has to move the sash or lid with its seals, and the voltage and current have to suit the panel. iComply uses the maker's published data for the existing unit and the replacement, and records both in the job notes.

On window AOVs, the opening angle and the distance the sash travels matter for the free area. Swapping to an actuator with a shorter stroke can quietly reduce the area the fire strategy relies on. That is why actuator replacements are written up with the stroke and opening recorded, not just ticked off.

A louvre AOV uses a bank of blades that rotate open on a signal. Louvres are common at the top of smoke shafts, in plant rooms and on facades where a window is not practical. The blades, the linkage and the actuator have to move together, and the free area depends on the blade angle when fully open.

A window AOV is an opening window fitted with an actuator so it can open automatically for smoke ventilation. It is the most common AOV in blocks of flats, usually on the stair or at the end of a corridor. The window must open far enough, in the right direction, to give the free area the fire strategy relies on.

commercial-aov-installation.body:
An automatic opening vent, usually shortened to AOV, is a window, roof hatch or louvre that opens on a signal so smoke can leave a common stair, corridor or lobby. In most blocks the signal comes from a smoke detector on the same level or from the fire alarm panel. The vent itself is only one part of the job. The actuator, the control panel, the battery standby, the cabling and the firefighter override switch all have to work together before the vent does what the fire strategy expects.

Most AOVs in residential blocks sit at the head of the stair or on each corridor. Guidance in Approved Document B for common stairs and corridors in flats refers to minimum free areas, commonly quoted as 1.0 m² at the stair head and 1.5 m² for a corridor or lobby vent. The fire strategy for the building decides what applies. iComply records the vent size and opening as measured on site and does not assume a free area that has not been checked against the drawings or the maker's data.

An AOV that will not open is a fire-safety defect, not a cosmetic one. The responsible person under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 has to keep fire-safety equipment in efficient working order. That covers smoke vents. In practice it means a written test regime, a log of faults and someone competent to put them right. iComply writes the scope for that work and quotes it on application.

AOV work is often split between people who never meet. A window installer fits the frame, an electrician runs the cables, a fire-alarm contractor programmes the panel and a managing agent books the tests. iComply prefers one written scope that names every interface, so a vent that fails on test has an owner and a fix rather than a chain of emails.

AOV repair starts with finding the cause. A symptom — something that will not open, will not close, shows a fault or makes a noise — can have several causes. The fault is reproduced on site and traced before any part is ordered, so the repair fixes the problem rather than a guess.

After a repair, the AOV is tested in normal operation, and any related safety function is retested. The record shows the fault found, the cause, the repair and the test result.

Recurring faults are treated differently from one-offs. If the same fault keeps coming back, the record history is reviewed and the root cause is looked for — a supply problem, a damaged part elsewhere, an installation issue — rather than resetting it again.

The AOV control panel is the brain of a smoke-vent system. It reads the detectors, drives the actuators, charges the standby battery and reports faults. When the panel fails, every vent it controls is suspect, which is why panel faults are treated as priority defects in most fire-safety files.

An AOV system is everything that has to happen between a smoke detector seeing smoke and a vent standing open. That chain normally runs from detector to control panel, from panel to actuator, and from actuator to vent leaf or hatch. A standby battery keeps it alive when the mains fails. A firefighter switch lets the fire service take over. If one link is weak the whole system fails its test.

commercial-aov-installer.body:

Guidance in Approved Document B for common stairs and corridors in flats refers to minimum free areas, commonly quoted as 1.0 m² at the stair head and 1.5 m² for a corridor or lobby vent. The fire strategy for the building decides what applies. iComply records the vent size and opening as measured on site and does not assume a free area that has not been checked against the drawings or the maker's data.

The sequence on a typical natural smoke shaft or stair system is simple to describe and easy to get wrong. A detector sees smoke. The panel opens the vent on the fire floor and the vent at the top of the stair or shaft. Lift and door interfaces may follow. A firefighter switch at ground level lets the fire service open or close vents by hand. Each step is tested on its own and then end to end, and the result is written down.

Common faults on older AOVs include a dead standby battery, a seized chain actuator, a vent that opens but will not close, a detector head painted over during redecoration and a panel showing a fault that nobody has reset. None of these is unusual. What matters is that the fault is logged, isolated where needed, and repaired with parts that match the original performance rather than whatever happens to fit.

Choosing a AOV installer is mostly about how they handle the parts before and after the fitting. A good installer measures before ordering, names the product and its published data, explains interfaces with other systems, and leaves a written record at the end.

IComply acts as installer from its Stockport workshop for sites across the UK mainland. It does not claim accreditation badges it does not hold. What it offers is a written scope, products chosen from manufacturer data, and a handover record the next engineer can use.

commercial-louvre-aov-installation.body:

The blades, the linkage and the actuator have to move together, and the free area depends on the blade angle when fully open.

Louvre faults often start with the linkage. A pivot seizes, a blade drops, or the drive arm slips on its shaft. The actuator then strains against a stuck blade or runs without moving it. Louvres sit on the outside of the building, so access is part of the scope. Insect mesh, bird guards and debris all reduce the free area of a louvre. They are recorded as found. Where a mesh has been added after commissioning, the effect on free area is a question for the fire strategy and the maker's data, not something to guess on site.

A louvre AOV that closes poorly lets rain and draughts into the shaft, which then damages detectors and actuators lower down. Sealing and closing are checked alongside opening, because the long-term reliability of the whole system depends on it.

Roof smoke vents and hatches lift a lid on an actuator or gas strut. The upstand, seal, hinge and actuator are all checked. Roof access is planned before the visit, because it is often the hardest part of the job.

Products are tested and classified against the relevant part.

An installer working to EN 12101 is really working to the product's tested configuration. A ventilator tested at one size with one actuator is not automatically covered at another size with another actuator. iComply checks that what is fitted matches what the maker's documents show.

Classification details — such as reliability cycles, opening under load or temperature class — come from the maker's declaration of performance. They are quoted from those documents, never invented. Where documents are not available, that is recorded.

factory-aov-actuator-installation.body:
The actuator is the motor that physically opens and closes the vent. Chain actuators push window sashes outwards. Linear or spindle actuators lift roof hatches and louvre blades. Each one is sized by its maker for a force, a stroke and a supply voltage, and those published figures decide which actuator suits which vent.

Most actuator faults show up as a vent that opens slowly, opens part-way, stalls or will not close. Causes include a worn chain, a bent bracket, a sash that has dropped on its hinges, paint on the slide, or low voltage at the end of a long cable run. The fix depends on the cause, so the vent is opened and closed under test before any part is ordered.

Replacing an actuator means matching the original performance, not just the mounting holes. The stroke has to deliver the required opening, the force has to move the sash or lid with its seals, and the voltage and current have to suit the panel. iComply uses the maker's published data for the existing unit and the replacement, and records both in the job notes.

Some actuators include limit switches or feedback that tells the panel the vent has opened. Where that feedback exists, it is tested. A vent that opens but does not report open will show a fault, and a vent that reports open without moving is worse. Both are checked on the visit.

Seals, hinges and handles age. A window that has dropped on its hinges catches on the frame and the actuator stalls. A handle that has been locked shut by a resident or cleaner stops the vent opening at all. These simple faults are checked first.

Installation is quoted after measurement and product selection from published data.
factory-aov-panel-installation.body:
The AOV control panel is the brain of a smoke-vent system. It reads the detectors, drives the actuators, charges the standby battery and reports faults. When the panel fails, every vent it controls is suspect, which is why panel faults are treated as priority defects in most fire-safety files.

A panel replacement is rarely a straight swap. The new panel has to drive the same actuators at the right voltage and current, accept the existing detector and fire-alarm signals, and fit the space available. iComply records the existing panel, the number of outputs in use, the actuator loads and the battery size before recommending anything.

Batteries inside smoke-control panels have a service life set by the maker. They are replaced on condition and age, not when the panel finally gives up. The survey notes the battery date, the charger output and the standby test result, so the responsible person can plan the change rather than react to it.

Panel location matters. Panels are often fitted in a riser, a plant room or a landing cupboard. Access for testing, a clear label, a fault indicator that someone actually sees and a log book nearby make the difference between a fault that is reported and one that sits for months. These points go into the scope as well as the electrics.

Firefighter override switches connect to the panel and are tested with it. Keys go missing, labels fade and switches get painted. The override is part of the panel scope: is it there, is it labelled, does it open and close the vents it should, and can the fire service reach it at the entry point?

Installation of a AOV panel starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

On the day, installation covers fixing, wiring or mechanical setting-up, and the checks that prove the AOV panel works as intended. The maker's installation instructions are followed, and any departure needed for the site is written down with the reason.

Installation ends with handover: a record of what was fitted, where, with which settings, and the test results. The responsible person or site owner gets that record for their file, along with any maker's documentation supplied with the product.

Occupied buildings and live sites need planning. Access, isolation, residents or staff, and deliveries are agreed in advance. Where work has to be phased, the scope sets out the phases and what stays in service during each one.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A AOV panel that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.

Commissioning a AOV panel proves that it works as designed, in the building it is installed in, with the interfaces it depends on. It is more than switching on: every function is tested, every interface is proved and the results are recorded.

Commissioning works from a written cause-and-effect or functional description. Where none exists, one is drawn up from the design and agreed before testing starts, so everyone knows what a pass looks like.

Results are recorded item by item. Failures are fixed and retested, and the record shows both. The final commissioning record goes into the building's file with the maker's documentation.

Recommissioning is needed after significant changes: a new panel, a change of interface, an extension. The scope says what will be retested and why.

The actuator is the motor that physically opens and closes the vent. Chain actuators push window sashes outwards. Linear or spindle actuators lift roof hatches and louvre blades. Each one is sized by its maker for a force, a stroke and a supply voltage, and those published figures decide which actuator suits which vent.

An AOV system is everything that has to happen between a smoke detector seeing smoke and a vent standing open. That chain normally runs from detector to control panel, from panel to actuator, and from actuator to vent leaf or hatch. A standby battery keeps it alive when the mains fails. A firefighter switch lets the fire service take over. If one link is weak the whole system fails its test.

Factories and warehouses often use natural smoke and heat exhaust ventilation through roof ventilators, sometimes with smoke curtains dividing the roof into reservoirs. A AOV panel in this setting usually covers large roof areas and heavy-duty actuators.

Roof access is the main planning item: fragile sheets, rooflights, edge protection and safe access routes. Work at height is planned before the visit and written into the scope.

Changes to racking, mezzanines and partitions can change how smoke moves. Changes seen on site are reported for review.

Industrial sites often run shifts. Visits are planned with the site manager around production and deliveries.

Quotes are price on application. iComply does not publish catalogue prices for smoke-control work because two buildings with the same vent can need very different access, testing and interface work. The written scope sets out what is included so the price can be judged fairly.

Where a building's fire strategy is unclear or missing, iComply records what is installed and how it behaves and recommends the responsible person consult a fire engineer on design questions. Design decisions are not made on the fly during a service visit.

factory-louvre-aov-installation.body:
A louvre AOV uses a bank of blades that rotate open on a signal. Louvres are common at the top of smoke shafts, in plant rooms and on facades where a window is not practical. The blades, the linkage and the actuator have to move together, and the free area depends on the blade angle when fully open.

Louvre faults often start with the linkage. A pivot seizes, a blade drops, or the drive arm slips on its shaft. The actuator then strains against a stuck blade or runs without moving it. The survey opens and closes the louvre under test and looks along the full blade set rather than only at the motor.

Insect mesh, bird guards and debris all reduce the free area of a louvre. They are recorded as found. Where a mesh has been added after commissioning, the effect on free area is a question for the fire strategy and the maker's data, not something to guess on site.

A louvre AOV that closes poorly lets rain and draughts into the shaft, which then damages detectors and actuators lower down. Sealing and closing are checked alongside opening, because the long-term reliability of the whole system depends on it.

When louvres are replaced, the new unit's published free area and size are compared with the original. A louvre that looks the same can have a different blade profile. iComply writes the comparison into the scope so the responsible person can see the basis of the choice.

fire-rated-aov-installation.body:
A fire-rated AOV is a vent or door that both opens for smoke ventilation and forms part of a fire-resisting construction when closed, for example a shaft door or a vent in a protected wall. Its fire resistance comes from tested assemblies, so the frame, leaf, seals and hardware must match the tested configuration.

Fire-rated AOVs fail in two ways: they do not open, or they do not close and seal. Both matter. The vent is tested open and closed, and seals, gaps and closing devices are inspected against what the maker's data shows.

Changing any part of a fire-rated AOV — actuator, bracket, seal or glazing — can affect its fire performance. Replacement parts are chosen from the maker's published data for that assembly, and the change is recorded.

Penetrations around fire-rated vents are a common weakness. Cable entries, actuator fixings and frame gaps are inspected for fire stopping where they can be seen. Gaps are reported.

Installation of a new fire-rated AOV follows the maker's instructions for the tested assembly, including the wall type and fixings. iComply confirms the substrate and opening size on site before quoting.

An installer working to EN 12101 is really working to the product's tested configuration. A ventilator tested at one size with one actuator is not automatically covered at another size with another actuator. iComply checks that what is fitted matches what the maker's documents show.

Window AOVs and roof AOVs behave differently. A window vent relies on the actuator pushing the sash out to a set angle, so the opening distance and the hinge position matter. A roof hatch or smoke vent lifts a lid, so access to the roof, the weight of the lid and the condition of the upstand matter. iComply notes which type is installed before anyone talks about parts, because the survey method is different.

Typical buildings include purpose-built blocks of flats, converted houses split into flats, care homes, student accommodation, offices, hotels, mixed-use schemes, warehouses and enclosed car parks. Each has its own fire strategy and its own constraints on access.

Smoke control interacts with the fire alarm, door closers, lifts and sometimes the building management system. The visit records those interfaces so faults that cross between systems are traced to the right place.

hmo-aov-actuator-installation.body:
The actuator is the motor that physically opens and closes the vent. Chain actuators push window sashes outwards. Linear or spindle actuators lift roof hatches and louvre blades. Each one is sized by its maker for a force, a stroke and a supply voltage, and those published figures decide which actuator suits which vent.

Most actuator faults show up as a vent that opens slowly, opens part-way, stalls or will not close. Causes include a worn chain, a bent bracket, a sash that has dropped on its hinges, paint on the slide, or low voltage at the end of a long cable run. The fix depends on the cause, so the vent is opened and closed under test before any part is ordered.

Replacing an actuator means matching the original performance, not just the mounting holes. The stroke has to deliver the required opening, the force has to move the sash or lid with its seals, and the voltage and current have to suit the panel. iComply uses the maker's published data for the existing unit and the replacement, and records both in the job notes.

Brackets and fixings are part of the actuator job. A strong motor on a weak bracket will tear itself out of the frame. The survey looks at the frame material, the bracket condition and the fixing method, and notes where a frame repair or a different bracket is needed.

Service visits are booked in advance and planned around access. The engineer arrives with the previous record so trends and repeat issues can be followed up rather than rediscovered.

During a service, worn or failing parts are noted with a recommended action. Small adjustments are made on the day; larger repairs are quoted separately on application so the client can approve them.

Service contracts can cover a single site or a portfolio. The scope sets out what each visit covers, how often visits happen and how faults found between visits are handled.

Panel location matters. Panels are often fitted in a riser, a plant room or a landing cupboard. Access for testing, a clear label, a fault indicator that someone actually sees and a log book nearby make the difference between a fault that is reported and one that sits for months. These points go into the scope as well as the electrics.

A louvre AOV uses a bank of blades that rotate open on a signal. Louvres are common at the top of smoke shafts, in plant rooms and on facades where a window is not practical. The blades, the linkage and the actuator have to move together, and the free area depends on the blade angle when fully open.

Common faults on older AOVs include a dead standby battery, a seized chain actuator, a vent that opens but will not close, a detector head painted over during redecoration and a panel showing a fault that nobody has reset. None of these is unusual. What matters is that the fault is logged, isolated where needed, and repaired with parts that match the original performance rather than whatever happens to fit.

Window AOVs and roof AOVs behave differently. A window vent relies on the actuator pushing the sash out to a set angle, so the opening distance and the hinge position matter. The survey notes the battery date, the charger output and the standby test result, so the responsible person can plan the change rather than react to it.

Panel location matters. Panels are often fitted in a riser, a plant room or a landing cupboard. Access for testing, a clear label, a fault indicator that someone actually sees and a log book nearby make the difference between a fault that is reported and one that sits for months. These points go into the scope as well as the electrics.

hmo-smoke-shaft-installation.body:
A smoke shaft is a vertical duct that runs the height of a building with a vent into each corridor and a vent or louvre at the top. On a signal, the vent on the fire floor and the top vent open so smoke rises up the shaft and out. Natural shafts rely on buoyancy; mechanical shafts use a fan.

Shaft performance depends on the vents opening on the correct floor only. If every corridor vent opens, smoke can be drawn into clean corridors. The cause-and-effect is checked floor by floor so the fire floor opens and the others stay shut.

Shaft vents are usually dampers or doors with actuators. They need to seal when closed and open fully when called. Each is tested, and the shaft head vent or louvre is checked for blockages, debris and mesh.

manual-barrier.body:
A manual barrier is a vehicle barrier that someone opens and closes by hand. Most are counterbalanced, so the arm lifts with modest effort and stays up or down where it is put. They are locked with a padlock, a key-operated catch or a drop-in pin. There is no motor, no control board and no mains supply, which is why manual barriers suit sites where access is occasional and controlled by a keyholder.

Manual versus automatic is mostly a question of traffic and control. A manual barrier works well when a handful of authorised people use the entrance each day and someone can be relied on to lock it. Once vehicles arrive throughout the day, or drivers keep leaving the arm up because getting out of the car to lift it is a nuisance, an automatic rising-arm barrier with a fob, keypad, intercom or ANPR becomes the practical choice.

Typical sites for manual barriers include private car parks, residential estates, warehouse yards, depots, farm and estate tracks, utility compounds and service roads that need to stay closed most of the time. They are also used as a temporary or secondary closure behind an automatic barrier for out-of-hours lockdown.

Counterbalance is what makes a manual barrier safe to use. A weight or spring offsets the arm so it does not slam down or spring up. When an arm is replaced, shortened, or fitted with a skirt, reflectors or a sign, the balance changes. An arm that drops on its own, or needs two people to lift, is a sign the balance has gone and needs adjusting before someone is hurt.

This page sets out what a manual barrier is, where it is used and what decides whether it suits a particular building or entrance. It is written for landlords, managing agents, facilities managers and site owners who need to make a decision and want the facts first.

The first step with any manual barrier is to describe the site: the address, the building or entrance, who uses it and what is installed now. Photos and rough measurements help. iComply then confirms what a visit would look at and what would be left out.

Options are set out side by side in a written scope. Where there is a choice between products, the published manufacturer data for each is named so the comparison is fair. Prices are on application once the scope is agreed.

Existing equipment is recorded before anything new is proposed. Often a repair, an adjustment or a change of part solves the problem without a full replacement, and the scope says so plainly.

Manual barrier repair starts with finding the cause. A symptom — something that will not open, will not close, shows a fault or makes a noise — can have several causes. The fault is reproduced on site and traced before any part is ordered, so the repair fixes the problem rather than a guess.

Repairs use parts that match the original performance from the maker's published data, or a documented equivalent where the original is no longer available. The part used and the reason for the choice are written in the job record.

After a repair, the manual barrier is tested in normal operation, and any related safety function is retested. The record shows the fault found, the cause, the repair and the test result.

Arm skirts hang below the arm to discourage pedestrians and cyclists from ducking underneath. They add weight and catch air, and they need clearance from the ground when the arm is down. Where a skirt is wanted, it is included in the balance calculation and the arm length is checked against the manufacturer's published limits with the skirt fitted.

Swing-type manual height barriers pivot on one post and lock to the other. The swing arc has to clear kerbs, walls and parked vehicles, and the locking point needs to be reachable from the ground. The hinge, padlock or key cylinder and the receiving bracket are the parts that wear and get damaged.

Barrier work is usually instructed by a site owner, managing agent, facilities manager or estate manager. On shared sites, the reply confirms who else needs to agree the scope — for example a freeholder or a residents' company.

Typical sites include private car parks, residential estates, office and retail car parks, warehouse yards, depots, schools, hospitals, farms and private access roads. Each has its own traffic, users and constraints.

Barriers sit where vehicles and pedestrians meet. The layout keeps people out of the arm's path where possible, with a separate footway and clear markings.

Manual barrier installation sets the post on a foundation sized for the ground, fits the arm cut to the measured clear opening, sets the counterbalance, fits the rest post and locking points, and checks the arm clears kerbs and parked vehicles through its full movement.

A manual barrier is a vehicle barrier that someone opens and closes by hand. Most are counterbalanced, so the arm lifts with modest effort and stays up or down where it is put. They are locked with a padlock, a key-operated catch or a drop-in pin. There is no motor, no control board and no mains supply, which is why manual barriers suit sites where access is occasional and controlled by a keyholder.

Counterbalance is what makes a manual barrier safe to use. A weight or spring offsets the arm so it does not slam down or spring up. When an arm is replaced, shortened, or fitted with a skirt, reflectors or a sign, the balance changes. An arm that drops on its own, or needs two people to lift, is a sign the balance has gone and needs adjusting before someone is hurt.

Installing a manual barrier means setting the post on a proper foundation, fitting a receiver or rest post at the far end, checking the arm swings or lifts clear of kerbs, walls and parked cars, and fitting the locking points. The clear opening width is measured on site and the arm is cut or supplied to suit, not the other way round.

Repairs on manual barriers are usually mechanical: a seized pivot, a bent arm, a broken counterweight bracket, a lost key, a rotten timber arm or a post loosened by a vehicle strike. Servicing covers greasing pivots, checking the counterbalance, tightening fixings, checking locks and replacing worn reflective strips so the arm stays visible.

Installation of a manual barrier starts with a survey, not a delivery. The site is measured, the existing equipment and interfaces are recorded, and the product is chosen from the maker's published data to suit what was found. Nothing is ordered until the scope is written and agreed.

Interfaces are where installations go wrong. A manual barrier that depends on a fire alarm, an access-control system or a power supply from another contractor is only as good as that link. The interface is named in the scope and tested at handover.
