reinforced-barrier-arm.body:
A reinforced barrier arm resists bending and casual damage better than a light aluminium section, which suits busy yards and depots. It is heavier, so the operator or manual counterbalance must be able to handle it — checked against the manufacturer's published data — and it is not described as impact-rated unless the maker publishes that classification.

A heavy-duty manual barrier uses a stronger post, a heavier or reinforced arm and more robust locking than a light-duty barrier. It suits depots, yards, industrial estates and sites where the barrier is used often or takes the occasional knock from vehicles.

A reinforced barrier arm is usually steel or a reinforced section rather than light aluminium. It resists bending and casual damage, but it also weighs more, so the counterbalance and post must suit the heavier arm.

Heavy-duty does not mean crash-rated. Impact-tested vehicle security barriers are a different category with published test classifications. iComply does not describe a barrier as crash-rated unless the manufacturer publishes that classification for the model fitted.

Foundations for heavy-duty barriers are sized for the post and arm. The ground is checked on site, and the foundation is set accordingly.

Heavy-duty arms are measured to the clear opening, cut or supplied to length, and balanced on installation. Any later change — a skirt, sign, light or reflector — means re-balancing.

Servicing covers pivots, counterbalance, locks, fixings and foundations, with a check for bending or corrosion along the arm.

Heavy-duty manual barriers are often fitted with drop-in locking pins or hasps that take a closed-shackle padlock. These resist casual tampering better than light catches and are chosen where the barrier secures a yard overnight.

Reinforced barrier arm replacement starts with recording what is there: the model, dimensions, fixings and settings. The replacement is chosen to match from the maker's published data, or to a new measured size if the site has changed.

Replacement is also a chance to check the rest of the installation. A replaced part on a worn mechanism will not last. The visit notes related wear and recommends any further work.

After replacement, the equipment is re-set, rebalanced or reconfigured as needed and tested. The record shows the old and new parts and the settings used.

Where a direct replacement is not available, an equivalent is chosen from published data and the reasons are recorded.

A maintenance visit covers visual inspection, cleaning where needed, mechanical and electrical checks, adjustment, functional testing and a written record. Defects found are listed with a recommended action and a priority.

Planned maintenance is cheaper and less disruptive than reactive repair. Worn parts are spotted before they fail, and replacements can be planned into budgets rather than bought in a hurry.

Maintenance records matter to insurers, auditors and the fire authority. iComply's records list each item checked, the result and any action, in a format that can be filed and compared visit to visit.

The frequency of maintenance depends on the equipment, how heavily it is used and what the building's documents require. iComply follows that frequency, or proposes one in writing where none has been set.

Counterbalance is what makes a manual barrier safe to use. A weight or spring offsets the arm so it does not slam down or spring up. When an arm is replaced, shortened, or fitted with a skirt, reflectors or a sign, the balance changes. An arm that drops on its own, or needs two people to lift, is a sign the balance has gone and needs adjusting before someone is hurt.

The rest post is not an accessory on long arms. Supporting the free end stops the arm bending, bouncing or being pushed down by hand, and it takes load off the operator when the barrier is closed. Its position is set from the measured arm length and the kerb line, and its height is matched to the arm in the closed position.

Barrier work is usually instructed by a site owner, managing agent, facilities manager or estate manager. On shared sites, the reply confirms who else needs to agree the scope — for example a freeholder or a residents' company.

Typical sites include private car parks, residential estates, office and retail car parks, warehouse yards, depots, schools, hospitals, farms and private access roads. Each has its own traffic, users and constraints.

Barriers sit where vehicles and pedestrians meet. The layout keeps people out of the arm's path where possible, with a separate footway and clear markings.

Ground conditions decide foundations. Buried services are checked before any digging, and the barrier position may move to avoid them.

Signage and markings tell drivers what to expect: access method, height or width limit, contact details. They are part of the scope, not an afterthought.

Records list the barrier model, arm length, settings, measured clearances and test results, so future repairs and replacements start from facts.

Quotes are price on application. Barrier jobs vary with ground, cabling, access control and safety measures, so a catalogue price would mislead. The written scope lists measurements, products and exclusions so the price can be judged fairly.

To start, send the address, photos of the entrance from both directions, rough measurements of the opening and any headroom limits, how many vehicles use it and what you want the barrier to achieve. Phone 07517806082, use WhatsApp or the contact form.

Dimensions in a scope are either measured on site or taken from the manufacturer's published data for the named product. iComply never invents a product rating, and does not describe a barrier as impact-tested unless its maker publishes that classification.

The deeper barrier guides on this site cover manual barriers, arm length, height clearance and height restriction, and opening, lane and width restriction. Each links back to a written-scope approach and price on application.

A barrier specification is the written proposal that follows a survey. It names the barrier type, the operator model and its published arm range, the measured arm length, any height or width restriction, the access method, safety devices and signage.

A barrier survey records the measurements that decide what can be installed: the opening and clear widths, the headroom above the barrier position, the ground and foundations, buried services, kerbs and islands, turning space and the routes pedestrians use.

A barrier specification then turns those measurements into a written proposal: barrier type, arm length, operator model chosen from the manufacturer's published range, height or width restriction if required, access control method, safety devices and signage.

Specifications quote dimensions as site-measured or from the manufacturer's published data. They never invent a rating. Where a figure depends on a product choice, the product and its published range are named.

Swept-path analysis may be part of the survey where HGVs, coaches or long vehicles use the entrance. It shows whether the turn can be made with the barrier and islands in place.

For automatic barriers, the specification includes safety measures from a risk assessment: loops, photocells, safety edges and force limits, with BS EN 12453 as the usual reference for powered barriers.

The survey and specification are written documents that the client can take to other installers if they wish. The installation itself is quoted on application.

Photos alone rarely settle a barrier specification. They help plan the visit, but clearances, ground conditions and buried services need to be checked on site. The survey visit records each measurement with a photo of where it was taken.

This page sets out what a barrier specification is, where it is used and what decides whether it suits a particular building or entrance. It is written for landlords, managing agents, facilities managers and site owners who need to make a decision and want the facts first.

The first step with any barrier specification is to describe the site: the address, the building or entrance, who uses it and what is installed now. Photos and rough measurements help. iComply then confirms what a visit would look at and what would be left out.

manual-barrier-repair.body:
Manual barrier repairs usually involve the pivot, the counterbalance, the lock or the arm. An arm that drops on its own or needs two people to lift is a balance fault and is put right before the barrier is used again.

A manual barrier is a vehicle barrier that someone opens and closes by hand. Most are counterbalanced, so the arm lifts with modest effort and stays up or down where it is put. They are locked with a padlock, a key-operated catch or a drop-in pin. There is no motor, no control board and no mains supply, which is why manual barriers suit sites where access is occasional and controlled by a keyholder.

Manual versus automatic is mostly a question of traffic and control. A manual barrier works well when a handful of authorised people use the entrance each day and someone can be relied on to lock it. Once vehicles arrive throughout the day, or drivers keep leaving the arm up because getting out of the car to lift it is a nuisance, an automatic rising-arm barrier with a fob, keypad, intercom or ANPR becomes the practical choice.

Installing a manual barrier means setting the post on a proper foundation, fitting a receiver or rest post at the far end, checking the arm swings or lifts clear of kerbs, walls and parked cars, and fitting the locking points. The clear opening width is measured on site and the arm is cut or supplied to suit, not the other way round.

When to upgrade to automatic? If the barrier is left open because locking it is a nuisance, if keys are shared too widely to control, or if traffic has grown, an automatic barrier usually pays its way in actual security. iComply can survey for both and set out the difference in a written scope, price on application.

Manual barrier repair starts with finding the cause. A symptom — something that will not open, will not close, shows a fault or makes a noise — can have several causes. The fault is reproduced on site and traced before any part is ordered, so the repair fixes the problem rather than a guess.

Repairs use parts that match the original performance from the maker's published data, or a documented equivalent where the original is no longer available. The part used and the reason for the choice are written in the job record.

Some faults leave equipment unsafe or out of service. Where that happens, the equipment is made safe and the responsible person is told in writing what is out of service and what interim measures are needed until the repair is complete.

After a repair, the manual barrier is tested in normal operation, and any related safety function is retested. The record shows the fault found, the cause, the repair and the test result.

Recurring faults are treated differently from one-offs. If the same fault keeps coming back, the record history is reviewed and the root cause is looked for — a supply problem, a damaged part elsewhere, an installation issue — rather than resetting it again.

A manual height barrier is a fixed or swinging frame, usually a horizontal bar on two posts, that stops vehicles above a set height from entering. The manual version can be unlocked and swung open by a keyholder so an over-height vehicle — a refuse lorry, a removal van, a fire appliance or a delivery — can be let through when needed.

Arm skirts hang below the arm to discourage pedestrians and cyclists from ducking underneath. They add weight and catch air, and they need clearance from the ground when the arm is down. Where a skirt is wanted, it is included in the balance calculation and the arm length is checked against the manufacturer's published limits with the skirt fitted.

manual-barrier-arm-length.body:
Manual barrier arm length is limited by what a person can lift safely with the counterbalance doing most of the work. Manufacturers publish the arm lengths each manual barrier supports. Longer manual arms usually need a heavier counterweight or stronger spring and a rest post at the free end, and every change to the arm — cutting, a skirt, reflectors or a sign — means re-setting the balance so the arm neither drops nor springs up.

Barrier arm length starts with the clear opening width. The arm has to span from the barrier post to the far side of the opening, usually landing in a rest post or fork. The clear opening is measured on site between kerbs, walls or posts, and the arm length follows from that measurement plus the manufacturer's allowances for the post and rest.

Typical UK rising-arm barriers are supplied with arms roughly in the 3 m to 8 m range, depending on the model. These are ranges, not product claims. Each manufacturer publishes the arm lengths each operator supports, and the model is chosen from those published figures for the measured opening.

Longer arms need more from the barrier. The operator must be rated by its maker for the arm length, the springs or counterbalance must suit the arm weight, and long arms usually need a rest post at the free end so the arm is supported when closed. Skimping on any of these leads to a barrier that strains, bounces or wears out early.

Accessories change the arm's weight and balance. A skirt, LED lights, reflectors, a sign or an articulated joint all add weight. After any of these is added, or after an arm is shortened, the barrier is re-balanced so it opens and closes as its maker intends.

Arms can be shortened to suit a narrower opening, but not indefinitely. Shortening changes the balance and may move the arm outside the range the springs are set for. The springs or counterweights are adjusted, or changed, to suit the new length.

height-restriction-barrier.body:
A height restriction barrier stops vehicles above a set height from entering an area. It is usually a horizontal bar or frame on two posts across the entrance to a car park, estate road, yard or undercroft. Its job is to protect a low structure, keep large vehicles out of a car-only area, or prevent unauthorised overnight parking by vans and caravans.

The restriction height is measured, not guessed. It is set from the lowest point the site needs to protect, with a margin agreed in the scope, and the measured maximum height is shown on signage at the barrier and on the approach so drivers can stop or turn in time.

Height barriers come as fixed, swing-open and lockable types. A fixed frame suits sites that never need tall vehicles in. A swing or lockable barrier lets a keyholder open the restriction for refuse lorries, removals, maintenance or emergency vehicles.

Vehicle classes drive the decision. A car-only car park may set the restriction just above typical car and small-van height. A site allowing vans but not HGVs sets it higher. The vehicles the site wants to admit are listed in the scope so the height can be justified.

Height barriers are frequently paired with a rising-arm barrier: the height bar stops a tall vehicle before it reaches the entrance, and the rising arm controls who enters. Spacing between the two allows a car to wait without blocking the road and gives tall vehicles room to turn.

articulated-arm-barrier.body:
An articulated arm barrier has a hinged arm that folds part-way along its length as it rises. Because the outer section stays roughly horizontal or folds back, the arm needs much less headroom than a straight arm of the same length. It is the usual answer for undercroft car parks, basements and entrances under canopies.

The fold point and the folded height are published by the manufacturer for each model and arm length. The site's ceiling height and obstructions are measured and compared with those figures before an articulated arm is specified.

Articulated arms carry extra moving parts — the hinge, the linkage and sometimes a guide. These need regular checks and lubrication, and they are more vulnerable to damage if a vehicle strikes the arm.

Balancing an articulated arm is more involved than a straight arm. Springs are set for the specific arm length and fold configuration, and any change needs re-balancing.

Articulated arms are often used with lighting or reflective strips for visibility in dim car parks. These add weight and are allowed for in the balance.

Installation and servicing record the arm length, fold point, measured headroom and spring setting for future work.

Articulated arms are heavier and more complex than straight arms of the same length, so the operator must list the articulated configuration in its published data. Not every operator that accepts a straight arm of a given length accepts an articulated one.

Accessories change the arm's weight and balance. A skirt, LED lights, reflectors, a sign or an articulated joint all add weight. After any of these is added, or after an arm is shortened, the barrier is re-balanced so it opens and closes as its maker intends.

At this span, two opposing shorter arms are worth comparing, because they halve the load on each operator, need less headroom and leave half the entrance usable if one barrier is out of service. The clear opening is measured on site before either option is quoted.

Barrier arm length starts with the clear opening width. The arm has to span from the barrier post to the far side of the opening, usually landing in a rest post or fork. The clear opening is measured on site between kerbs, walls or posts, and the arm length follows from that measurement plus the manufacturer's allowances for the post and rest.

Typical UK rising-arm barriers are supplied with arms roughly in the 3 m to 8 m range, depending on the model. These are ranges, not product claims. Each manufacturer publishes the arm lengths each operator supports, and the model is chosen from those published figures for the measured opening.

Longer arms need more from the barrier. The operator must be rated by its maker for the arm length, the springs or counterbalance must suit the arm weight, and long arms usually need a rest post at the free end so the arm is supported when closed. Skimping on any of these leads to a barrier that strains, bounces or wears out early.

Accessories change the arm's weight and balance. A skirt, LED lights, reflectors, a sign or an articulated joint all add weight. After any of these is added, or after an arm is shortened, the barrier is re-balanced so it opens and closes as its maker intends.

Arms can be shortened to suit a narrower opening, but not indefinitely. Shortening changes the balance and may move the arm outside the range the springs are set for. The springs or counterweights are adjusted, or changed, to suit the new length.

Options are set out side by side in a written scope. Where there is a choice between products, the published manufacturer data for each is named so the comparison is fair. Prices are on application once the scope is agreed.

Existing equipment is recorded before anything new is proposed. Often a repair, an adjustment or a change of part solves the problem without a full replacement, and the scope says so plainly.

Headroom matters: the arm needs vertical space roughly equal to its length when open. Where the ceiling is low, an articulated or swing arm may be needed.

Safety on powered barriers comes from a risk assessment. Detection loops, photocells, safety edges and force limits are used as needed, with BS EN 12453 as the usual reference. Pedestrians are kept away from the arm's path with a separate footway where possible.

Common faults include worn springs, failed loops, damaged arms, control board faults and access-control interface problems. Each is diagnosed on site before parts are ordered.

Servicing covers the operator, springs, arm, loops, photocells, access control and signage, with safety tests recorded.

Duty cycle is how often a barrier can open and close in an hour or a day without overheating or wearing out early. Busy entrances need barriers with a published duty suited to the traffic. The expected number of vehicles is written into the scope so the operator can be matched to it.

How long should my barrier arm be?
Long enough to span the measured clear opening into a rest post, within the arm range the manufacturer publishes for the chosen operator.
Why does a long arm need a rest post?
To support the free end when closed, so the arm does not bend or bounce and the operator is not overloaded.
Do I need to rebalance after adding a skirt or lights?
Yes. Any added weight, or shortening, changes the balance, so springs or counterweights are re-set.
How do you choose a barrier arm replacement?
By matching the existing model, dimensions and fixings from published data, or a new measured size if the site has changed.
